demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
I remind myself it could have been worse
try hard not think about the trauma

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I should have protected others and I failed

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water
issues.explanation: Water/flooding triggers are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another in a car accident, given the rest of the profile centers on crash-related and guilt/shame themes. This trigger introduces a different threat context without support from memory or appraisal items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Feelings: Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Feelings' is internally incoherent as worded: 'Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion' describes the opposite of avoidance. Within the maladaptive strategies node, it directly conflicts with an avoidance strategy.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body
issues.explanation: 'Body Unreliable' fits poorly with the rest of the profile for a perpetration-type accident trauma in which the patient's appraisals otherwise center on guilt, humiliation, and shattered beliefs. There are no memory, trigger, or strategy items suggesting bodily injury, panic/somatic threat, or physical incapacity to support this appraisal.

vignette:
Rajesh, a 42-year-old tax inspector, had never imagined that a routine drive to a client’s office would unravel everything he believed about himself. One rainy evening, as he approached an intersection, a child darted between parked cars. His reflexes were too slow; the thud against the front bumper, the scream that cut through the rain, the sight of the small body lying still on the asphalt—these fragments were seared into him, but not as a coherent whole. Some moments were impossibly clear: the wet sound of the impact, the mother’s wail that seemed to come from inside his own head. Others were blank, like a missing reel of film. He later learned the child survived but with severe brain injuries. Rajesh was never charged; the police ruled it an unavoidable accident. But that verdict meant nothing to him.

In the weeks that followed, Rajesh found that certain encounters scraped open the wound without warning. Spotting a dented fender on the street or hearing a squeal of brakes would flood him with the same auditory intrusion—a sound he could not unhear, a voice yelling that he had done this. Funerals, even for people he did not know, became unbearable; the sight of a hearse or a grave made his chest tighten because it felt as though the child’s funeral was happening over and over. And if a colleague or his wife, Priya, ever mentioned the word “accident” in passing, Rajesh would go rigid, desperate to escape the conversation. These triggers were not random—they were cues that threatened to complete the incomplete picture, to force him to see what he had blocked out. He came to believe that remembering the event fully would confirm he was a monster, so he tried to push the thoughts away. Yet the more he suppressed, the more the triggers seemed to multiply: a car honking, a client’s file involving a personal injury claim, even the smell of wet asphalt. The suppression itself turned every mundane moment into an ambush.

He developed quiet, private rituals of punishment. Driving was impossible; he took the bus, but even then he would sit with his eyes closed through entire stretches, telling himself he deserved the nausea that came with each sway. At home, he would replay the moment and whisper, “I should have protected them. I failed.” Whenever the guilt grew too sharp, he would counter it with a downward comparison: *At least the child is alive. It could have been worse.* That thought provided a moment of relief, but it also left him feeling treacherous—as if he were excusing himself. So he spun back into self-blame, the cycle tightening. His occupation as a tax inspector became a minefield: he processed claims for accident-related medical expenses, and each line item brought the child’s hospital stay into his mind. He stopped reviewing those files, claiming a stomach bug, and asked a coworker to cover them. The avoidance cost him time and credibility, but the alternative felt worse.

His memory of the event remained fragmented, a collage of hyper-clarity and void. He could hear the impact but could not picture the child’s face from before the moment of contact. Because the memory returned in such visceral fragments, he began to see reminders of the accident everywhere—a child’s laughter in a grocery aisle, a blue sedan parked outside his window, the metallic smell of rain on pavement—each one a potential ambush he could not afford to ignore. That blankness terrified him because it felt like a moral failing—if he had been a better person, he would remember everything, would take full responsibility. And this belief that the gaps in his memory were proof of his guilt kept pulling him back into those same fragmented images, making the flashes of recall come more frequently and feel more accusing, as though his own mind was holding up evidence against him. Instead, his shame whispered that he was hiding from the truth even inside his own mind. The partial clarity reinforced his shattered belief that the world was not safe or just; if a careful driver could destroy a family in an instant, then nothing made sense. And the humiliation was constant: he felt branded, as though everyone at the tax office could see the cowardice stamped on his forehead. He had always taken pride in being dependable; now he was the man who hurt a child and could not even look at a graveyard.

By the time Rajesh walked into the clinic, he had not driven in four months, had stopped attending family gatherings for fear someone would mention the accident, and had lost ten pounds from the constant knot in his stomach. What finally brought him was a moment at work: a photograph of a boy in a wheelchair on a discarded tax form had triggered a panic attack so severe he had to lock himself in the bathroom. He was terrified that his wife was beginning to see him as broken, that his children would learn what he had done and be ashamed. He hoped, more than anything, that someone could help him find a way to live with the weight he carried—or, if that was not possible, at least to quiet the sounds in his head long enough to sleep through a single night.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not convey that the memory influences or leads to triggers; instead, triggers cue memory, and suppression leads to more triggers.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
